title: Hugging Face NLP Course
description: Free course on using transformer models for NLP, covering the pipeline API, tokenizers, datasets, fine-tuning, and sharing models.
quality_notes: Written by the maintainers of the library it teaches, so it reflects that ecosystem's conventions rather than a neutral survey of approaches.
why_useful: Gets you to a working fine-tuned model quickly while still explaining tokenisation and the training loop, rather than hiding both behind a one-line API call.
learning_outcomes: Use pretrained models for common NLP tasks
Explain what a tokenizer produces and why it matters
Fine-tune a transformer on your own dataset

title: Transformers documentation
description: Official documentation for the Transformers library, covering model classes, pipelines, training, generation strategies and task-specific guides.
quality_notes: A reference to consult by task, not to read through.
why_useful: The canonical reference for the library most NLP work is built on, including generation parameters that are otherwise a common source of confusing behaviour.
learning_outcomes: Find the right model class and API for a task
Control generation with the available decoding parameters
Understand the training utilities the library provides

title: Tokenization algorithms
description: Official explanation of subword tokenisation approaches, comparing byte-pair encoding, WordPiece, Unigram and SentencePiece and how each builds a vocabulary.
why_useful: Tokenisation is where most people's mental model of a language model first breaks. This explains subwords before embeddings, which is the order that makes later behaviour predictable.
learning_outcomes: Explain why subword tokenisation exists
Compare BPE, WordPiece and Unigram approaches
Predict how vocabulary size trades off against sequence length

title: spaCy 101: Everything you need to know
description: Official introduction to spaCy covering the processing pipeline, linguistic annotations, tokenisation, named entities, word vectors and the Doc/Span/Token data structures.
why_useful: A reminder that plenty of production NLP is well served by fast pipeline components rather than a large model, and the fastest way to get entities out of text today.
learning_outcomes: Process text through a linguistic pipeline
Extract entities, spans and part-of-speech tags
Decide when a lightweight pipeline beats a transformer

title: Advanced NLP with spaCy
description: Free interactive online course with in-browser exercises covering data structures, statistical models, rule-based matching, pipelines and training your own components.
author: Ines Montani
why_useful: Exercises run in the browser with immediate feedback, so the concepts are practised rather than read — rare among free NLP courses.
learning_outcomes: Write rule-based matchers for structured extraction
Build and customise a processing pipeline
Train a component on your own annotated data

title: Speech and Language Processing
description: Comprehensive NLP textbook covering regular expressions, n-gram and neural language models, sequence labelling, parsing, semantics, machine translation, dialogue and speech.
author: Dan Jurafsky, James H. Martin
quality_notes: Published as draft chapters that are revised over time; check the site for which chapters are current before relying on a specific one.
why_useful: The standard reference for the field, and the one that keeps the pre-neural foundations of NLP in view rather than treating the subject as beginning with transformers.
learning_outcomes: Understand language modelling from n-grams to neural models
Work with sequence labelling and parsing formalisms
Place modern methods in the context of the field's history

title: Stanford CS224N: Natural Language Processing with Deep Learning
description: University course covering word vectors, neural networks for NLP, recurrent models, attention, transformers, pretraining, and natural language generation.
quality_notes: Which materials are publicly available varies by year. Assignments and lecture recordings are not guaranteed to be posted for the current offering.
why_useful: The reference university treatment of modern NLP, with assignments that require implementing the ideas rather than calling a library that already has.
learning_outcomes: Derive and implement word embedding methods
Explain the progression from RNNs through attention to transformers
Reason about pretraining objectives and their effects

title: The Illustrated Word2vec
description: Visual explanation of word embeddings, covering the intuition behind distributed representations, skip-gram training, and negative sampling.
author: Jay Alammar
quality_notes: Community-created explainer rather than an official or peer-reviewed source.
why_useful: Embeddings underpin search, retrieval and RAG, and this builds the intuition for why vector similarity corresponds to meaning before any of that machinery appears.
learning_outcomes: Explain what an embedding vector represents
Describe how skip-gram training produces useful vectors
Reason about similarity in embedding space

title: Sentence Transformers documentation
description: Official documentation for computing sentence and text embeddings, covering pretrained models, semantic search, clustering, and training custom embedding models.
why_useful: The practical toolkit for turning the idea of embeddings into a working semantic search or retrieval component, which is the foundation any RAG system stands on.
learning_outcomes: Generate sentence embeddings with a pretrained model
Build a semantic search index over your own documents
Understand when to fine-tune an embedding model

title: BERT: Pre-training of Deep Bidirectional Transformers for Language Understanding
description: The paper introducing BERT, a bidirectional transformer encoder pretrained with masked language modelling and next-sentence prediction, then fine-tuned per task.
why_useful: Established the pretrain-then-fine-tune pattern that still shapes how NLP systems are built, and remains the clearest statement of why bidirectional context matters.
learning_outcomes: Explain masked language modelling as a pretraining objective
Describe the pretrain then fine-tune workflow
Distinguish encoder-only from decoder-only model families
